# Fire Water System Control Narrative

**System:** FP-1 (diesel), FP-2 (electric), JP-1 (jockey), header pressure PT-601

**Document purpose:** Define the control boundary between the listed fire pump controllers and the site PLC/SCADA, and correct the draft control intent.

**Status:** Draft for review by the Engineer of Record, the AHJ and the insurer (e.g., FM Global, if applicable). Clause references are to NFPA 20 and NFPA 25 in general terms. Confirm them against the adopted editions and any site or insurer standards (e.g., FM DS 3-7, API 2030, NFPA 30).

---

## 1. Summary of Corrections to the Client's Draft

| # | Draft intent | Correction | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | PLC starts fire pumps on low header pressure | **The listed controllers start the pumps.** Each controller uses its own pressure sensing line and transducer. The PLC is not in the automatic start path. PT-601 is used for monitoring, alarming and trending only. | NFPA 20 requires automatic starting by the listed controller's own pressure-actuated means. A PLC failure or network fault must not be able to prevent a start. |
| 2 | PLC stops pumps after pressure recovers for 10 minutes | **The PLC never stops a fire pump.** Stopping is manual, at the controller. If automatic shutdown is used at all, it is a controller function with its minimum run timer set to at least 10 min for FP-2 (electric) and at least **30 min for FP-1 (diesel)**. **Recommended setting: manual stop only** for both pumps. | NFPA 20 does not allow remote stopping. It does not allow automatic shutdown where the pump is the sole supply for sprinkler or standpipe systems, or where the AHJ requires manual shutdown. Petrochemical terminals with deluge and foam systems normally fall in that case. |
| 3 | PLC trips FP-1 on low lube oil pressure and high coolant temperature | **No trip on either condition.** Both are **alarm only**. The only automatic engine shutdown permitted is **overspeed**, provided by the listed diesel controller and engine (typically about 120% of rated speed, with manual reset at the controller). | NFPA 20 philosophy is that the engine runs to destruction during a fire. Protecting the engine is not allowed to take priority over delivering fire water. |
| 4 | (Implied) PLC is the alarm system of record | **Supervisory signals must go to the listed fire alarm control panel (FACP)** or a constantly attended location as NFPA 72 and NFPA 20 require. The PLC receives parallel, isolated contacts for SCADA visibility only. | NFPA 20 and NFPA 72 |

---

## 2. Control Philosophy

1. **The listed controllers are autonomous.** FP-1 and FP-2 start, run and (if ever permitted) stop entirely through their own listed controllers. They do so without power, logic or communications from the site PLC.
2. **The PLC is monitor-only toward the fire pumps.** It may read status, alarm, log and trend. Its only permitted output to the fire pumps is an optional remote start (Section 5.4).
3. **The PLC must not:**
   - stop a pump
   - inhibit a start
   - place a controller in OFF or MANUAL
   - change setpoints
   - command the ATS
   - load-shed the fire pump
4. **Signal isolation.** All signals from the controllers to the PLC use dry contacts (or listed communication cards in read-only mode), wired so that no fault in PLC wiring can affect controller operation.
5. **Failure mode.** Loss of the PLC, SCADA, network or PLC power must have **no effect** on fire pump availability.

---

## 3. Equipment and Control Boundaries

| Item | Controlled by | PLC role |
|---|---|---|
| FP-1 diesel, 2500 gpm @ 150 psi | Listed diesel fire pump controller: own pressure transducer and sensing line, dual battery sets and chargers, crank cycle, weekly test timer, pressure recorder | Monitor and alarm; optional remote start |
| FP-2 electric, 2500 gpm @ 150 psi | Listed electric fire pump controller with listed fire pump ATS: own pressure transducer and sensing line, weekly test timer, pressure recorder | Monitor and alarm; optional remote start |
| JP-1 jockey | Jockey pump controller with its own pressure switch or transducer and sensing line | Monitor and alarm (run status, excessive starts) |
| PT-601 header pressure | Site instrument | Indication, alarming, trending, discrepancy checks. **Not a start signal.** |
| LT-610 diesel day tank level | Site instrument | Level indication and low-level alarm |
| Pump room temperature | Site instrument | Low and high temperature alarms |

**Sensing lines.**
- Each controller (FP-1, FP-2, JP-1) has an **independent sensing line**, not shared.
- Each line is taken between the pump discharge check valve and the discharge control valve.
- Each line has the check valves or orifice unions NFPA 20 requires.
- No isolation valve may be installed that could isolate the controller from system pressure.

---

## 4. Pressure Setpoints

| Function | Setpoint (psig) | Where set |
|---|---|---|
| JP-1 stop | 165 | Jockey controller |
| JP-1 start | 155 | Jockey controller |
| FP-2 (electric, lead) start | 145 | FP-2 controller |
| FP-1 (diesel, lag) start | 135 | FP-1 controller |

**Comments on the proposed setpoints:**

- **Spacing is acceptable.** The 10 psi steps meet or exceed NFPA 20 Annex guidance:
  - lead pump start about 5 psi below jockey start
  - each additional pump about 10 psi lower
  - jockey start about 10 psi below jockey stop

  Electric lead and diesel lag is a reasonable arrangement.
- **Verify the jockey stop pressure against churn.** Annex guidance sets jockey stop at fire pump churn plus minimum static suction pressure. A 150 psi rated pump may churn anywhere up to 140% of rated, i.e. about 160 to 210 psi. Obtain the certified pump curve and reconcile 165 psig with it.
- **Verify the system pressure rating.** Maximum pump discharge is churn plus maximum static suction, and for the diesel it is also affected by engine overspeed (up to 121% of net rated shutoff in NFPA 20 terms). If that can exceed the rating of system components (often 175 psi for sprinkler components), a pressure relief valve or higher-rated components are required. **This is a design check for the EOR, not a PLC item.**
- **Sequential start timers.** Set them in the controllers, in addition to the pressure stagger, so that both pumps cannot start at the same moment on a rapid pressure drop. Typical values are FP-2 at 0 s and FP-1 at 10 s; confirm against the controller manual and NFPA 20.
- **Matching PLC alarm thresholds.** PLC alarm thresholds on PT-601 should mirror these values (Section 6) so that discrepancies can be detected.

---

## 5. Sequences of Operation

### 5.1 Normal Standby

- All controllers are in **AUTO**.
- JP-1 holds the header between 155 and 165 psig.
- FP-2 is on normal utility power, with the ATS in the normal position.
- FP-1 has both batteries charged and the engine jacket heater on.
- The PLC shows "Fire Water System Normal" when no supervisory or trouble signals are active.

### 5.2 Jockey Pump Operation

1. Pressure falls to 155 psig. The JP-1 controller starts JP-1.
2. JP-1 runs until 165 psig, plus any minimum run timer set in its controller to prevent short cycling. The timer is set per the controller manufacturer and EOR.
3. PLC monitoring:
   - counts JP-1 starts per hour and per 24 h
   - raises **"JP-1 Excessive Starts"** above the configured limit (site to set; this indicates a leak or a passing valve)
   - raises **"JP-1 Long Run"** if JP-1 runs continuously longer than a set time (for example 30 min; site to set)

### 5.3 Automatic Fire Pump Start

**FP-2 (electric, lead):**
1. Header pressure falls to 145 psig at the FP-2 controller's own transducer.
2. The FP-2 controller starts FP-2 after its sequential start delay.
3. FP-2 runs until it is stopped manually at the controller (Section 5.5).
4. If FP-2 fails to start, its controller annunciates "Fail to Start" and the condition is reported to the FACP and the PLC.

**FP-1 (diesel, lag):**
1. Header pressure falls to 135 psig at the FP-1 controller's own transducer.
2. The FP-1 controller starts FP-1 after its sequential start delay. It runs its listed crank cycle: typically six attempts of about 15 s crank and 15 s rest, alternating batteries.
3. If the engine does not start, the controller raises "Fail to Start" / "Overcrank".
4. Once running, FP-1 runs until it is stopped manually at the controller.
5. The **only** automatic shutdown is overspeed, which requires manual reset at the controller.

**PLC actions during an automatic start (monitor only):**
- Annunciate "FP-2 Running" and/or "FP-1 Running" as a priority alarm on SCADA.
- Record the event start time and the PT-601 pressure at start.
- Discrepancy alarms (Section 6):
  - PT-601 is at or below 140 psig for more than 15 s and FP-2 is not running.
  - PT-601 is at or below 130 psig for more than 25 s and FP-1 is not running.

  The deadbands and delays are to be tuned at commissioning. These alarms are **diagnostic only and take no action**.
- Trend PT-601, pump run status and LT-610 continuously during the event.

### 5.4 Remote and Manual Starts

- **Local manual start:** at each controller, using its start pushbutton or emergency run mechanism. FP-1 also has a manual crank selector.
- **Deluge or foam system start (if applicable):** where the design requires the fire pumps to start when deluge valves operate, use the controller's listed deluge-valve start input. That input is wired from the deluge valve or releasing panel, **not** through the PLC.
- **Optional SCADA remote start:**
  - The PLC may drive an interposing relay wired to the controller's listed remote start input. This is a start command only.
  - It requires operator confirmation on the HMI.
  - The circuit must be wired so that a PLC fault cannot inhibit an automatic start or hold a pump stopped.
  - **There is no remote stop.**

### 5.5 Stopping

- **Stopping is manual only, at the controller.** An operator presses the controller's stop pushbutton, or for FP-1 uses the engine stop, after the incident commander confirms the fire water demand has ended.
- **Automatic shutdown is disabled in both controllers.** If the AHJ ever approves it for a specific case, it remains a controller function:
  - minimum run timer of at least 10 min for FP-2
  - minimum run timer of at least 30 min for FP-1
  - starting cause must have returned to normal
  - applies only after an automatic start
- **The PLC has no stop function**, no "pressure recovered for X minutes" logic, and no ability to place a controller in OFF.

### 5.6 FP-2 Power Transfer (ATS)

- The listed fire pump transfer switch transfers automatically on loss or degradation of normal power to the alternate source (on-site generator or second utility feed).
- The PLC and any site load management system **must not** command the ATS, shed FP-2 from the generator, or block retransfer.
- If the generator is shared, FP-2 must be in the highest-priority load block and is never sheddable.
- PLC monitoring:
  - **"FP-2 On Alternate Source"**: supervisory
  - **"FP-2 Normal Power Failure / Phase Reversal"**: trouble
  - **"ATS Alternate Source Not Available"**: trouble

### 5.7 Weekly / Periodic Test

- The controller weekly test timers start each pump without flow (churn test) at different times:
  - **FP-1:** at least 30 min run, weekly (per NFPA 25)
  - **FP-2:** at least 10 min run, weekly or monthly as permitted by NFPA 25 and the AHJ
- The controller pressure recorders log the start pressure. Operators still attend the test per NFPA 25.
- PLC actions:
  - flag test runs separately from demand runs (time-of-week window plus an operator "Test in Progress" acknowledgment)
  - record run duration and suction/discharge pressure (if instrumented)
  - record LT-610 before and after
- Weekly tests end by controller timer or by manual stop at the controller, **not by the PLC**.

---

## 6. PLC Monitoring and Alarm List

Every supervisory or trouble signal below that NFPA 20 or NFPA 72 requires must also go to the **FACP**. The PLC receives isolated parallel contacts.

### FP-1 Diesel Controller

| Signal | Class | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Engine running | Alarm (priority) | |
| Controller not in AUTO (OFF/MANUAL) | Supervisory | |
| Fail to start / overcrank | Alarm | Pump unavailable |
| Overspeed shutdown | Alarm | Manual reset at controller |
| Low lube oil pressure | **Alarm only, no trip** | |
| High coolant temperature | **Alarm only, no trip** | |
| Battery 1 / Battery 2 failure | Trouble | |
| Battery charger failure | Trouble | |
| ECM / fuel injection malfunction (electronic engines) | Trouble | If equipped |
| Low engine jacket temperature (heater failure) | Trouble | |
| Low suction or low raw cooling water pressure/flow | Trouble | If applicable to the cooling arrangement |
| Common engine/controller trouble | Trouble | |

### FP-2 Electric Controller and ATS

| Signal | Class |
|---|---|
| Motor running | Alarm (priority) |
| Fail to start | Alarm |
| Loss of phase / phase reversal / power failure | Trouble |
| On alternate source | Supervisory |
| Alternate source not available | Trouble |
| Controller not in AUTO / isolating switch open | Supervisory |
| Common controller trouble | Trouble |

### JP-1

| Signal | Class |
|---|---|
| Running | Status |
| Excessive starts (PLC-derived) | Trouble |
| Long run (PLC-derived) | Trouble |
| Controller fault / not in AUTO | Trouble |

### Site Instruments

| Tag | Signal | Setpoint (to confirm) | Class |
|---|---|---|---|
| PT-601 | Header low pressure | 150 psig (below JP-1 start, above FP-2 start) | Trouble |
| PT-601 | Header low-low pressure | 140 psig | Alarm |
| PT-601 | Header high pressure | Below system component rating | Alarm |
| PT-601 | Transmitter fault / out of range | 4-20 mA under or over range | Trouble |
| PT-601 | FP-2 start discrepancy | ≤140 psig, FP-2 not running, 15 s | Alarm |
| PT-601 | FP-1 start discrepancy | ≤130 psig, FP-1 not running, 25 s | Alarm |
| LT-610 | Low fuel level | At or below **2/3 of tank capacity** (NFPA 20 low-fuel signal requirement; confirm against edition) | Supervisory |
| LT-610 | Low-low fuel level | Site to set, e.g. remaining run time under 4 h at full load | Alarm |
| LT-610 | High level / overfill | Below tank overfill point | Alarm |
| TT (pump room) | Low temperature | 40 °F (4 °C) minimum. For the diesel room, use the engine manufacturer's minimum if it is higher (often about 70 °F / 21 °C for starting). | Supervisory |
| TT (pump room) | High temperature | Site to set, per engine and electrical equipment ratings | Trouble |

**Fuel tank sizing note:** NFPA 20 requires fuel for 8 h at full load, typically 1 gal/hp plus 5% for expansion plus 5% for sump. Diesel fuel for FP-1 must be reserved exclusively for FP-1. The PLC must not control any fuel transfer that could draw down FP-1's tank.

---

## 7. Prohibited PLC Functions (Consolidated)

The PLC/SCADA shall **not**:

1. Provide the primary automatic start signal for any fire pump.
2. Stop, trip or shut down any fire pump for any reason, including:
   - pressure recovery
   - low oil pressure
   - high coolant temperature
   - high or low fuel level
   - pump room temperature
   - ESD
3. Inhibit or delay a fire pump start, or place a controller in OFF or MANUAL.
4. Change controller setpoints or timers.
5. Command the fire pump ATS or shed FP-2 from emergency power.
6. Include fire pumps in a plant ESD or fire-and-gas trip matrix as a tripped device. Fire and gas logic may **start** pumps only through a listed remote start input.

---

## 8. Items to Confirm Before Issue

1. Adopted editions of NFPA 20, NFPA 25 and NFPA 72, plus AHJ and insurer requirements, including whether automatic shutdown is prohibited outright (assumed here).
2. Certified pump curves, churn pressure and maximum static suction. Reconcile the jockey stop pressure and check whether a pressure relief valve is needed (Section 4).
3. Whether a deluge or foam start is required, and its wiring path.
4. Whether a SCADA remote start is wanted, and its HMI confirmation scheme.
5. Generator load management arrangement for FP-2.
6. Diesel engine manufacturer's minimum room temperature and jacket heater arrangement.
7. FACP interface: which signals go to the FACP and which go to the PLC only.
8. Commissioning tuning of the PT-601 discrepancy alarm thresholds and delays.
